weeks.title: Week 1-3: The Journey Begins
weeks.babyDevelopment: Conception and implantation happen during these first weeks. There's no visible baby yet — pregnancy dating begins from the first day of your partner's last menstrual period. The fertilized egg travels down the fallopian tube and implants into the uterine lining around day 6-10.
weeks.partnerExperience: Your partner likely doesn't know she's pregnant yet. There are no noticeable symptoms at this stage, though some women report mild cramping during implantation.
howToHelp: Confirm the pregnancy together when the time comes
Start taking prenatal vitamins together as a show of solidarity
Have an open conversation about your feelings and readiness
Begin tracking her cycle if you're actively trying to conceive

actionItems.text: Research prenatal vitamins (600 mcg folic acid, 27 mg iron)
Have a conversation about parenting goals and expectations
Start saving — aim for a 6-month emergency fund

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Is this really happening?

weeks.title: Week 4: Poppy Seed
weeks.babyDevelopment: The embryo is tiny but mighty. The amniotic sac and early placenta are forming. The embryo has two layers of cells that will develop into all organs and body parts. This is when a home pregnancy test can first detect the pregnancy.
weeks.partnerExperience: A missed period is the first major sign. Fatigue may set in as progesterone levels surge. Some women feel nothing yet; others notice tender breasts or mild nausea.
howToHelp: Be present when she takes the pregnancy test
Schedule the first prenatal visit together (typically weeks 8-10)
Start adjusting household routines to support her rest
Begin researching what to expect in the coming weeks

Discuss when and how to share the news with family
Review your health insurance maternity coverage

weeks.commonDadQuestion: When do we tell people?

weeks.title: Week 5: Peppercorn
weeks.babyDevelopment: The neural tube — which becomes the brain and spinal cord — is forming. A tiny heart starts beating at about 110 beats per minute. The circulatory system is the first major system to function. Three layers of cells are differentiating into all body systems.
weeks.partnerExperience: Nausea may begin as hCG levels double every 48-72 hours. Morning sickness is a misnomer — it can strike any time of day. Fatigue is intensifying as the body works overtime building the placenta.
howToHelp: Stock nausea-friendly foods: crackers, ginger ale, bland snacks
Keep food smells minimal — take over cooking if needed
Be patient with her energy levels
Place crackers on the nightstand for morning nausea

actionItems.text: Stock the pantry with nausea-friendly foods

Start a shared note for questions to ask the doctor

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Is morning sickness normal?

weeks.title: Week 6: Pomegranate Seed
weeks.babyDevelopment: Arm and leg buds are appearing. Blood circulation begins. Early structures for ears, eyes, and mouth are forming. The embryo has a curved, tadpole-like shape. The heart is beating steadily and can sometimes be seen on an early ultrasound.
weeks.partnerExperience: Morning sickness is in full swing for many women. Heightened sense of smell can trigger nausea. Extreme fatigue is common as the body diverts energy to building the baby's life support system.
howToHelp: Take over cooking duties — food smells can be a major trigger
Help identify specific nausea triggers and avoid them
Don't take her mood changes personally — hormones are surging
Offer to handle more household chores without being asked

Research what your insurance covers for prenatal care
Start reading about pregnancy and fatherhood

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What if she can't keep food down?

weeks.title: Week 7: Blueberry
weeks.babyDevelopment: Bones are beginning to replace cartilage. The brain is growing rapidly, generating about 100 new cells per minute. Tiny nostrils and mouth are visible. Arm buds now look like paddles that will form hands.
weeks.partnerExperience: Nausea often intensifies this week. She may have strong food aversions and cravings. Emotional mood swings are common as hormones peak. Fatigue continues to be overwhelming.
howToHelp: Help identify specific nausea triggers — keep a log together
Offer small, frequent meals instead of three large ones
Be her calm presence when emotions run high
Remember: mood swings are biological, not a choice

actionItems.text: Track nausea triggers together
Practice active listening when she shares how she feels
Research genetic testing options (NIPT, NT scan)

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Should we see a doctor about the nausea?

weeks.title: Week 8: Bean
weeks.babyDevelopment: All major organs and body systems are developing. The umbilical cord is fully formed. Fingers are beginning to form, though still webbed. The embryo is making spontaneous movements, though too small to feel. All four chambers of the heart are working.
weeks.partnerExperience: Nausea and fatigue often peak around this time. Frequent urination increases as the uterus presses on the bladder. She may feel bloated and her pants may feel tighter even though she's not showing.
howToHelp: Attend the first prenatal visit together — you'll hear the heartbeat
Prepare questions for the doctor in advance
Be ready for an emotional experience at the first ultrasound
Handle logistics so she can focus on resting

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What if we miscarry?

weeks.title: Week 9: Cherry
weeks.babyDevelopment: Teeth and taste buds are beginning to form beneath the gums. The embryo is starting to look more human — the tail is disappearing. Essential organs like the liver, kidneys, and brain continue developing rapidly. Tiny earlobes are visible.
weeks.partnerExperience: Frequent urination is increasing. Nausea may still be strong but could start easing for some. Emotional sensitivity is high. She may feel anxious about money and the future.
howToHelp: Review your health insurance plan together — understand deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums
Have an honest, calm conversation about finances
Reassure her that worrying is normal and you're a team
Continue managing household tasks proactively

weeks.title: Week 10: Kumquat
weeks.babyDevelopment: Fingers and toes are fully separated — no more webbing. The baby (now officially called a fetus) can bend limbs. Vital organs are formed and starting to function. Bone development is accelerating throughout the body.
weeks.partnerExperience: Nausea may be starting to ease for some women. Round ligament stretching can cause occasional sharp pains. Increased blood volume may make veins more visible. Energy is still low.

Support whatever decision she makes about testing
Start exploring childcare options — daycare waitlists can be 6-12 months
Continue being patient with fatigue and nausea

weeks.title: Week 11: Brussels Sprout
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby can open and close fists. Tooth buds are appearing under the gums. The head makes up about half the body length. Hair follicles are forming. The baby is starting to look distinctly human.
weeks.partnerExperience: Bloating and gas are common due to progesterone slowing digestion. She may be experiencing food cravings more intensely. Some women get a pregnancy glow from increased blood flow. Others break out.

Help her feel comfortable with body changes
Keep healthy snacks stocked for her cravings
Start thinking about how and when to tell your employer

weeks.title: Week 12: Lime
weeks.babyDevelopment: All organs, limbs, bones, and muscles are in place and continuing to develop. The baby can stretch, kick, and make breathing movements. Reflexes are developing — the baby will start to respond to touch. Miscarriage risk drops significantly after this week.
weeks.partnerExperience: Energy is often returning as the first trimester ends. Nausea may be fading. She might start showing slightly. This is often when couples feel ready to share the news.

Help plan how to announce the pregnancy
Start creating the baby registry together
Support her in telling friends and family when she's ready

weeks.title: Week 13: Peapod
weeks.babyDevelopment: Vocal cords are forming. The baby's unique fingerprints are developing. Intestines move from the umbilical cord into the abdomen. The end of the first trimester marks a major milestone — miscarriage risk drops dramatically.
weeks.partnerExperience: Appetite is increasing as nausea fades. She may feel a surge of relief and energy. The transition to the second trimester often brings improved mood and reduced anxiety.

Celebrate the end of the first trimester together
Start thinking about a babymoon or special trip during the second trimester

weeks.title: Week 14: Lemon
weeks.babyDevelopment: Welcome to the second trimester. Fingerprints are fully formed — your baby is already unique. The baby can make facial expressions like squinting and frowning. The body is catching up to the head in proportional size.
weeks.partnerExperience: Round ligament pain may begin — sharp pains on the sides of the abdomen as the uterus stretches. Energy levels are typically improving. The pregnancy brain fog some women experience may start.

Take advantage of her improved energy to do things together

weeks.title: Week 15: Apple
weeks.babyDevelopment: The lungs are developing and practicing breathing movements with amniotic fluid. The baby's skeleton is hardening from cartilage to bone. Taste buds are functional — the baby can taste what your partner eats through the amniotic fluid.
weeks.partnerExperience: Nasal congestion is common due to increased blood flow to mucous membranes. Back pain may begin as the center of gravity shifts. Skin changes like darkening of the nipples or a linea nigra line may appear.

Offer back rubs — they'll be increasingly appreciated

weeks.title: Week 16: Avocado
weeks.babyDevelopment: The ears can now hear sounds from outside the womb. The baby's eyes are sensitive to light even though the eyelids are still sealed. The circulatory and urinary systems are fully functioning. Toenails are starting to grow.
weeks.partnerExperience: Back pain is becoming more common. She may start feeling tiny flutters of movement, though first-time moms often don't notice until weeks 18-22. Sleep disturbances may begin as finding a comfortable position gets harder.

weeks.title: Week 17: Turnip
weeks.babyDevelopment: A waxy coating called vernix is forming to protect the baby's skin in the amniotic fluid. The umbilical cord is growing thicker and stronger. Fat stores are beginning to develop under the skin. The baby's skeleton is transitioning from soft cartilage to hardened bone.
weeks.partnerExperience: Increased vaginal discharge is normal and healthy. She may feel warmer than usual due to increased blood volume. Itchy skin on the stretching belly is common. Vivid dreams may begin.

weeks.title: Week 18: Bell Pepper
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby can hear sounds from outside the womb clearly now. Myelin — a protective coating — is forming around the nerves. If your baby is female, her uterus and fallopian tubes are formed. The baby is increasingly active and may respond to loud noises.
weeks.partnerExperience: First flutters (quickening) may be felt — like butterflies or gas bubbles. Not all women feel them this early, especially with a first pregnancy. Round ligament pain continues. Appetite is strong.

weeks.partnerExperience: Quickening is likely happening — she may feel definite kicks and movements. Round ligament pain, back aches, and hip pain are common. Her belly is clearly visible now. She may be adjusting to her changing body.

Eyebrows and eyelashes are growing. This week's anatomy scan provides a detailed look at the baby's development.

weeks.partnerExperience: Braxton Hicks contractions may start — practice contractions that are irregular and not painful. Swelling in ankles and feet is common by late afternoon. Heartburn may increase as the uterus pushes up on the stomach.

weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby is fully developed and ready for birth. Average weight is 7-9 pounds, length is 19-21 inches. The skull bones are not fused, allowing them to overlap slightly for delivery. Your baby is ready to meet you.
weeks.partnerExperience: Regular contractions may begin. Water may break. She may experience a rush of emotions — excitement, fear, anticipation. If labor doesn't start, the provider may discuss induction options around 41 weeks.
howToHelp: Support your partner through labor — be her advocate and comfort
Time contractions using the 5-1-1 rule
Call the hospital when it's time
Be present, calm, and encouraging — you've prepared for this

actionItems.text: Support partner through labor as her advocate

Be present, calm, and encouraging during delivery
Enjoy skin-to-skin contact when your baby arrives
